result: Photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons or their terminals in the BLA selectively promoted conditioned licking behavior only when paired with reward availability (Photostim-Reinforced sessions), but not during unreinforced sessions (Photostim-Unreinforced), and did not affect unconditioned behaviors.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the behavioral findings are 'solid' and 'robust,' but express significant confusion about interpretation. One reviewer states the findings are 'somewhat unclear' and questions what the increase in post-reward licking means, noting 'it is not clear to me what this increase in post-award licking might mean.' Another reviewer notes the behavioral data is 'somewhat less complete' than the neural data. The editor summarizes that behavioral evidence for uncued reward seeking is 'somewhat less complete.'

result: Control experiments showed that photostimulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons did not increase locomotion, did not modify innate location preference, and was not inherently reinforcing as measured by real-time place preference.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praise these control experiments. One reviewer notes 'There are a number of important control experiments performed to determine that the observed effects were not due to locomotor activity and that stimulating basal forebrain ACh neurons is not inherently reinforcing.' These findings are not questioned or critiqued.

result: Photostimulation caused modest pupil dilation that developed more slowly than licking behavior, with larger effects during Photostim-Reinforced than Photostim-Unreinforced sessions, suggesting arousal effects that are temporally distinct from conditioned responding.
evaluation: One reviewer expresses confusion about the pupil dilation data, stating 'I was confused by the pupil dilation data in Figure S4 as the authors seem to want to argue that this effect, although specific to the rewarded window as licking is, is independent of the licking behaviour as it develops more slowly than the behaviour.' The reviewer asks 'Does it indicate that stimulating basal forebrain ACh interneurons does both things (i.e. increases arousal AND conditioned responding in the absence of discrete stimuli) but that the two things are independent of each other?'

result: Muscarinic receptor antagonist (scopolamine) abolished photostimulation-induced licking and impaired responses to conditioned tones, while nicotinic receptor antagonist (mecamylamine) had no effect, demonstrating that muscarinic receptors are necessary for conditioned responding to cholinergic stimulation.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this pharmacology finding without critique. One reviewer summarizes 'The reward-driven licking behavior was also mitigated by systemic cholinergic receptor antagonists' as part of the study's strengths. No concerns are raised about these data.

result: GCaMP photometry showed that basal forebrain cholinergic neurons are physiologically active during conditioned responding (licking), even in the absence of discrete cues and prior to reward delivery.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these findings positively. One reviewer notes 'They found strong calcium signals when mice were licking and when the tone was present, but also reported signals when mice were spontaneously licking.' The findings are described as part of the 'solid' recording data. No concerns are raised about the photometry results.

result: ACh sensor measurements in the BLA showed increased ACh levels during conditioned responding (licking), both when licking triggered reward delivery and when licking occurred without subsequent reward.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these ACh sensor findings without critique. One reviewer summarizes 'By injecting a genetically encoded Acetylcholine (Ach) sensor directly into the Basolateral Amygdala (BLA), they showed that Ach signals were present when mice were engaged in licking, both during reward availability and for non-rewarded licks.' These findings are part of the 'solid' recording data.

result: Photostimulation of cholinergic terminals in the BLA evoked similar levels of ACh release in both Photostim-Unreinforced and Photostim-Reinforced sessions, suggesting that reward associations gate postsynaptic responses rather than presynaptically changing ACh release.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly highlight this as a key finding. One reviewer states 'Perhaps the most compelling new idea in this manuscript is that ACh may have different effects on network activity in the BLA, a conclusion based on the measurement of equivalent photo-stimulated ACh levels in BLA during rewarded vs. unrewarded lick bouts despite increased licking/consumption in the rewarded bouts.' The editor echoes this, noting the article provides 'compelling evidence that ACh may have different effects on network activity in the BLA depending on the state of the network during reward engagement.'

result: In vivo electrophysiology revealed that cholinergic photostimulation had reward-contingency-dependent effects on BLA neural activity (suppression during Photostim-Reinforced sessions, facilitation during Photostim-Unreinforced sessions), while dmPFC responses were similar across session types.
evaluation: Reviewers find these electrophysiology data compelling. One reviewer notes 'The electrophysiological data showing that overall firing of BLA neurons during licking was higher as a result of photostimulation during unreinforced, and lower as a result of photostimulation during reinforced, sessions is intriguing in this context, as is the contrast with the overall ACh-mediated stimulation of firing in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex.' The findings are described as 'solid, particularly those relating to the recordings.'

result: Ex vivo electrophysiology demonstrated that cholinergic terminal photostimulation suppressed BLA projection neurons via monosynaptic muscarinic signaling and facilitated GABAergic interneurons via nicotinic signaling, suggesting a circuit model where cholinergic inputs suppress BLA output through multiple pathways.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge these ex vivo findings positively. One reviewer notes 'The ex-vivo data presented showing that ACh depresses BLA neuron activity via muscarinic ACh receptors on glutamate neurons and nicotinic ACh receptors on GABA neurons, along with previous data in the field suggesting that ACh has divergent effects on neuronal firing rate depending on whether baseline firing is low (tonic) or high (phasic), provides intriguing hints as to the role of ACh in state-dependent modulation of BLA activity.' These findings are part of the 'solid' recording data.

result: The WoOT task design involved unsignaled, variable-interval windows of opportunity where mice could not predict reward delivery prior to licking, representing an operant variable-interval reinforcement schedule with limited hold.
evaluation: One reviewer directly challenges the characterization of the task as operant, stating 'I do not think the behaviour in this task can be classed as operant - it is still a good task and still fine for detecting conditioned responding, but it cannot determine whether the responding is governed by a response-outcome association in the absence of a stimulus-outcome association.' Another reviewer notes confusion about the task interpretation and requests 'some additional details of the task are needed for the field to be able to replicate these experiments.'

result: Immunohistochemistry confirmed that nearly 90% (88.9%) of ChR2-expressing neurons were cholinergic, as verified by ChAT immunoreactivity.
evaluation: This validation is acknowledged by reviewers without critique. One reviewer notes the experiments were 'well-executed and sufficiently powered.' No concerns are raised about the specificity of viral targeting.
